A memory-safety flaw in CPython can allow malicious AI model templates to escape code sandboxes and execute arbitrary code inside inference servers, according to security researchers at RunSybil.

“By exploiting this vulnerability, attackers could gain a foothold inside servers responsible for processing millions of user requests,” Darius Houle, a security researcher at RunSybil, wrote in a blog post. “They also could strike directly at the underlying cloud infrastructure hosting those workloads.”

The researchers demonstrated how a specially crafted model could exploit the flaw to bypass Jinja, a Python-based templating engine used to structure interactions between users and LLMs, sandbox protections, and execute code in the process of serving the model. item.title: 🟠 The CIO’s trust paradox: Your team may be more honest with AI than with you
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

As a leader, you’ve probably spent years nudging your managers to create psychological safety. After all, organizations benefit greatly when it feels safe to challenge the boss, surface bad news early, and say the uncomfortable thing before it becomes the expensive thing.

The Space Shuttle Challenger disaster of 1986 has become the canonical warning. Engineers raised concerns about the O-rings used in the solid rocket booster before launch. Their warnings were overruled by managers under schedule pressure. Seventy-three seconds after liftoff, seven astronauts were dead. The lesson still holds: When people are afraid to speak or are pressured to comply, organizations miss what they already know.

AI, however, is introducing a complication most leaders haven’t accounted for. Your employees now have another place to speak, and emerging research suggests they may be more willing to challenge a machine than a human leader, while another body of research challenges our assumptions about psychological safety itself.

item.description:

Every year, thousands of enterprise organizations walk into technology negotiations trapped by the same fundamental mistake: they negotiate a product instead of solving a problem.

Having advised over 2,000 enterprise customers annually on technology acquisition over two decades, I see this pattern play out daily. Purchasing committees meticulously list the specific features, software modules and server specs they think they need, converting their organizational requirements into a static shopping list. On paper, this strategy feels disciplined. It creates a standardized, predictable item that procurement can use to negotiate a line-item discount with providers.

When you buy a fixed product, you get the immediate, gratifying perception of a lower price. But that upfront discount can come at a hidden cost: you risk cutting yourself off from the disruptive innovation of emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI).

The flaw impacts the lightweight Alpine Linux, which is widely used for cloud Docker container images, as well as Linux distributions for embedded systems.

The security bug, dubbed *SSHole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158, was discovered by Ozgun Kultekin, a researcher with security testing firm Wakefield, and has existed for the past 10 years. item.description:

French regional banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa admitted Wednesday that attackers had accessed an internal account via an unnamed third-party service provider’s platform and transferred funds to other financial institutions. Those funds, it said, could have then been potentially converted to cryptocurrency by the thieves.

The day before, cryptocurrency news outlet CoinDesk reported that the attack had been detected on Monday by blockchain investigator ZachXBT, although at the time he did not identify the entity involved. On Wednesday, he identified the suspected victim as Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, which the banking group later confirmed. It did not, however, specify whether the stolen funds were originally in traditional currency or cryptocurrency.

item.title: 🔵 The open compute revolution: Why the C-suite is redefining the modern data center
item.description:

For years, the enterprise data center operated under a predictable, if restrictive, playbook. Siloed, proprietary hardware stacks dictated infrastructure life cycles, leaving CIOs locked into vendor ecosystems. Every hardware refresh meant navigating premium pricing, constrained supply chains, and artificial limitations on interoperability.

Today, that playbook is being rewritten. As AI, massive data analytics, and intense computational demands reshape corporate strategies, C-level executives are turning to Open Compute infrastructure. Originally pioneered by hyperscalers to manage massive scale efficiently, open hardware design has graduated to the enterprise. By decoupling software from proprietary hardware and embracing collaborative, community-driven standards, open compute is no longer just a technical preference—it is a strategic business imperative.

For the C-suite, transitioning to an open infrastructure model solves three critical pain points: accelerating technological agility, optimizing total cost of ownership (TCO), and meeting aggressive corporate sustainability targets.

item.title: 🟠 The unit of scale is not headcount
item.description:

Every platform leader I know is being asked the same question: How do you deliver more with less?

The usual answers are familiar: hire more people, add more process or ask the existing team to move faster.

All three miss the underlying constraint. Headcount is an input. Throughput is an outcome. Organizational complexity is a cost.

Adding people can increase capacity, but it also adds communication paths, onboarding, coordination and decision overhead. Adding process can create consistency, but it can also slow the decisions it was meant to improve. Asking a team to work harder eventually consumes the very capacity you are trying to increase.

Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately.
